name: DEVENS, J.
description: Concurred, argued that a recorded judgment lien is a constitutionally protected property interest requiring personal notice for junior lienholders in execution sales, but applied this rule prospectively only due to reliance on old standards and potential prejudice to intervenors.

name: Todd W. Eddins
description: Concurred, argued that the Hawaiʻi Constitution's due process clause requires recording of all custodial interrogations (in-station and feasible outside-station) to protect rights against self-incrimination, confrontation, and fair trial, and that this rule should apply retroactively to cases on direct review.

name: Recktenwald, C.J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part with the majority opinion.

name: Richard W. Pollack
description: Concurred, arguing that the circuit court failed to provide adequate notice and opportunity to be heard, lacked specific findings for sealing, and erred in requiring Grube to retain counsel for his personal constitutional right of access.

name: EDDINS, J.
description: Concurred, arguing that the Hawaiʻi Constitution requires a strict separation of church and state, and the State's deed restriction requiring land use for church purposes only violates this principle by advancing religion.

name: Lisa M. Ginoza
description: Concurred, argued that HRS § 657-1.8(a) is a statute of limitations and does not violate the ex post facto clause, and that while the jury instructions were erroneous, the error was harmless given the defendant's admissions.

name: MCKENNA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the ultimate inquiry for "interrogation" under the Hawaiʻi Constitution is whether a law enforcement officer knew or should have known their words or conduct were reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response, even if normally attendant to arrest and custody.

name: MCKENNA, J.
description: Concurred, arguing that the Commission failed to justify its instream flow standards decisions, did not adequately protect Native Hawaiian rights, lacked transparent calculations, and unlawfully delegated its public trust duties, thus requiring vacatur and remand.

name: Mark E. Recktenwald, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the state's constitutional and statutory provisions do not violate the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments, and that the indictment was sufficient under the liberal construction standard because Tran was not prejudiced and the charge stated a crime.

name: MCKENNA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the State's 2018 designation of the MKAR as a state highway was a new claim not precluded by Act 14 of 1995 and constituted a breach of trust due to failure to comply with HHCA requirements.

name: MCKENNA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that unabandoned possessions of houseless persons constitute property protected by the due process clause of the Hawai'i Constitution, requiring notice and an opportunity to be heard, which was violated by the County's actions.

name: Todd W. Eddins
description: Concurred, argued that Hawaiʻi's Constitution and historical tradition do not support an individual right to carry deadly weapons in public, and that the challenged laws do not violate federal constitutional rights.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the anonymous jury violated defendants' constitutional rights to presumption of innocence, an impartial jury, effective assistance of counsel, and an impartial tribunal, constituting structural error that necessitates a new trial.

name: MCKENNA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Miranda warnings were required because Hewitt was in custody when probable cause developed, and even before, based on the totality of circumstances, overruling previous precedent that weakened this bright-line rule.

name: RECKTENWALD, C.J.
description: Concurred, arguing that the burden of proof remains with the challenging party, but the Ka Pa'akai framework applies to administrative rulemaking, requiring agencies to conduct a contemporaneous analysis of Native Hawaiian rights.

name: MCKENNA, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part, agreeing with most of the majority opinion but disagreeing with the requirement for agencies to engage in a contemporaneous Ka Pa'akai analysis during rulemaking.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Concurred, arguing that the State's unreasonable delay in sentencing deprived the defendant of due process and a fundamentally fair sentencing proceeding, and that the delay also deprived the defendant of the opportunity for allocution.

name: EDDINS, J.
description: Concurred, argued that HRS § 801-1 plainly requires a grand jury indictment for felony prosecutions and was not implicitly repealed.

name: MCKENNA, J.
description: Concurred with the majority's outcome, but also agreed with Justice Nakayama's constitutional argument that the State's prosecution was unconstitutional.

name: NAKAYAMA, J.
description: Concurred in the result of dismissing charges due to unconstitutional prosecution, but dissented from the majority's statutory interpretation, believing the 1982 amendment invalidated HRS § 801-1.

name: RECKTENWALD, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the 1982 constitutional amendment superseded HRS § 801-1, allowing felony charges via preliminary hearing.

name: RECKTENWALD, C.J.
description: Concurred, argued that the totality-of-the-circumstances test, where probable cause is relevant but not dispositive, is the correct standard for determining custody for Miranda warnings, and Sagapolutele-Silva was not in custody until after the SFST.

name: MCKENNA, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's decision overrules established precedent that provided a bright-line rule for Miranda warnings when probable cause exists, thereby reducing constitutional rights against self-incrimination.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's ruling weakens the constitutional protection against self-incrimination by removing the presumption that a person is not free to leave police custody when probable cause to arrest exists.

name: EDDINS, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the reapportionment commission has discretion in applying the "district within district" guidelines, as they are not mandatory restrictions but criteria to be considered, and the Plan is constitutional.

name: MCKENNA, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Commission was required to wholly include house districts within senatorial districts where practicable, and the majority failed to enforce the constitution's plain language and undermined the Hawaiʻi Constitution.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Commission was required to wholly include house districts within senatorial districts where practicable, and the majority failed to enforce the constitution's plain language and undermined the Hawaiʻi Constitution.

name: NAKAYAMA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the three readings requirement mandates that a bill retain some resemblance to earlier versions, and Act 84's non-germane amendment violated this by not restarting the readings.

name: RECKTENWALD, C.J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Constitution's plain language does not define what a "reading" entails or compel amendments to be germane, and the legislature's rules were properly followed.

name: CIRCUIT JUDGE KAWAMURA
description: Dissented, argued that the Constitution's plain language does not define what a "reading" entails or compel amendments to be germane, and the legislature's rules were properly followed.

name: McKenna, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part separately, arguing for different outcomes on specific sections of the petition.

name: Wilson, J.
description: Concurred in part and dissented in part separately, joining Justice McKenna as to Sections I and III.A.

name: Eddins, J.
description: Concurred separately, likely providing additional or distinct reasoning for the decision.

name: NAKAYAMA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the circuit court erred in suppressing evidence because Lee's independent actions severed the causal link between the officers' entry and the evidence, meaning it was not "fruit of the poisonous tree."

name: WILSON J.
description: Dissented, argued that the majority's decision creates a new suicide exception to the constitutional right to privacy, allowing warrantless entry into homes and bedrooms and significantly reducing privacy protections.
